The paper introduces a unified framework for reduction technique pipelines for survival analysis.
The authors provide an overview of the strengths, weaknesses, and applicability of the different reduction techniques to various survival tasks.
The authors provide a unified, user-friendly implementation of the reduction techniques that can be integrated into standard machine learning workflows.
The paper includes a quantitative benchmark comparison of the different reductions compared to established statistical and machine learning methods for survival analysis.
Piecewise exponential models (PEM) partition the time axis into intervals and estimate a constant or discrete-time hazard within each interval.
Discrete-time (DT) methods ignore the exact times at risk, relying solely on the interval index, making them simpler but potentially less precise than PEM.
Pseudo values (PV) transform the survival task into a regression problem by computing pseudo-values for the quantity of interest for each subject.

Censoring weighted binary classification (IPCW) transforms the survival task into a series of binary classification problems, where the goal is to predict whether an event occurs in each time interval.

The continuous ranking method (CRM) can directly model the full event time distribution by transforming the survival task into a regression problem to predict the cumulative distribution function of the event times.
The paper discusses software implementations of the reduction techniques, particularly in a machine learning context.

The authors illustrate the application of the respective reduction techniques to selected data examples, followed by a quantitative comparison to established statistical and machine learning methods for survival analysis.
The paper summarizes the results and limitations of the reduction techniques and provides ideas for future avenues of research.
The authors categorize survival tasks into two main dimensions: the type of censoring or truncation, and the number and type of events observed.
The paper covers single-event, recurrent events, and competing risks settings as special cases of the more general multi-state setting.
The authors discuss how left-truncation, time-varying features, and time-varying effects can be naturally incorporated into the reduction techniques through data transformations.
